item.title: Jumbo Package: Ryan Grubb faces the media after disaster in Knoxville
item.description: Things are getting mighty uncomfortable in Tuscaloosa
item.content:encoded:
Let’s start from the top, and get through the media appearances from the two coordinators and head coach.

First up is Ryan Grubb, who is pretty much public enemy #1 in the state of Alabama right now.

On the identity of the offense: 

“Our identity is to be able to get our playmakers the ball in space. I think we’re a good gap run team. We’ve shown that. We showed it on Saturday. We had some good gap scheme, inside zone and duo. That’s where it starts up front, getting the double teams, getting four hands on their biggest players, and then exploiting the secondary area where we think their weakest players are.”

I’m glad one of the reporters asked this, and it’s interesting to me what Grubb said.

“be able to get our playmakers the ball in space”

And yet, that’s not really what we’ve seen for the last two seasons from the passing game. Instead, Grubb has tended more towards a mid-range to deeper passing attack that doesn’t often lend to getting the receivers much room to get yards after catch.

I have seen this year’s offense put their identity on the gap, inside zone, and duo runs (even if he went away from it last week), so that tracks. But leading off with the comment about getting playmakers in space just doesn’t really feel what they’ve actually been doing.

One reporter asked him about the opening script, and Grubb did mention that the first play of the game was an RPO that got tipped.

Personally, I’m getting more and more out-of-favor with RPOs as a whole as defenses are getting better at figuring out the binary options and forcing offenses into decisions, rather than the other way around. But that’s a conversation for a different day.

On the decision to play off ball or play press in perimeter defense: “Well, you know, I mean, that’s one of the things that we have to constantly do, right, is you mix coverages in. We probably played more Cover 2 to the field this week than what we had just because you know they were throwing some of those perimeter screens out there, and so we we rolled up to that side and took some of them away at times. But there were other times, right, when number two is on, number one is off. You can’t be in press man in that situation because you’re going to get rubbed and picked. And then they were doing a lot of crack concepts into the boundary that we didn’t feel like we wanted to be in man against some of those structures as well. But you know, you just got to continue to mix those things throughout, and then you got to execute when the ball is thrown on the perimeter. Our guys have done a really nice job of that. We’ve done a nice job improving our screens, but we had four times that we did not execute well in those situations, and gave up two explosives, one being that fourth quarter drive on a on a first-and-19. It just cannot happen.”

This was an interesting answer from Wommack about the screen passes. He’s right, the Tide secondary has been really good against WR screens this year, so seeing them get outflanked on them multiple times last week was weird. And it sounds like it was something formationally with the way UT lined up the receivers. Overall, I think that the Alabama defense wasn’t bad necessarily. In fact, they kept this game from being something like a 41-3 blowout with their 1st half heroics. But ultimately, I felt like Wommack didn’t adjust to the situation or what Tennessee was doing and was sticking to a gameplan that would have been effective if the Tide had a lead, not trying to play from behind.

So, a mixed bag on my opinion on the defense, I guess.

On injury updates for Ryan Coleman-Williams, Racin Delgatty, Zabien Brown, Terrance Green and EJ Crowell: “A lot of these guys are kind of in the same boat. I’ll just go through. Zabien, lower leg injury, trying to evaluate throughout the week what he looks like. Racin is really in the same boat. So just kind of go to him. He’s progressing pretty well, though. And so, we’ll see. Gonna be week to week. Ryan is also, I mean, all these guys are kind of in the same area, the same window. I would not expect them to be practicing all week alone, but we’ll kind of see as the week gets to the end, what that looks like. EJ, lower leg injury, just kind of continue to evaluate. We’ll kind of see where he’s at in the next couple days. I wouldn’t expect him to practice early in the week for sure. And then Terrance is progressing. They’re all kind of kind of in the same spot. So, Terrance is week to week right now.”

Overall, I didn’t think DeBoer said much of anything out of left field. Chase Goodbread did press DeBoer on the play that’s making rounds with the Tennessee defender pointing out Marshall Pritchett right before the Tide ran a TE screen, and DeBoer mostly deflected that one.

I will say that I thought that, between the three coordinators, I thought the beat reporters did a much better job with asking questions to force answers, rather than their usual softball “how do you feel about X’s performance” that they seem to do every week.

As far as injury updates, I feel like DeBoer has been extra ambiguous this season, even compared to the last few years. So who knows if any of these guys are playing or what the injuries are.

Moving on to the upcoming week, this game against Texas A&M was supposed to be part of a brutal 4-game stretch for Alabama. Well, the first two proved to be just as brutal as we all expected, with Alabama not even looking like they belonged on the field against Tennessee. The good news is that the Aggies have barely looked like they belonged on the field this whole season, and if that trend continues, a game against a struggling Marcel Reed could be just what the doctor ordered for the Tide.

The Aggies have yet to score a touchdown on the road thus far in the 2026 season, and Reed has been a big issue in that stat, as the image shown above has become a little too frequent of an image for the 12th Man throughout 2026, as Reed has been sacked 12 times, including five times against the LSU Tigers.

However, head coach Mike Elko has remained steadfast in keeping Reed as the starter, saying that it simply would make no improvement to the team to take him out, even at where they currently are at this point in the 2026 season.

And this weekend, Reed is going to face a Crimson Tide defense that will test the part of his game that has been the shakiest this season, and that is staying out of trouble when the pocket collapses.

In addition to the dozen times that he’s been brought down, Reed has also completed just over half of his passes and before the game against The Citadel, his touchdowns and interceptions were the same number.

Not to mention, his passer rating is ranked near the bottom of all qualifying FBS quarterbacks, a stark contrast to where Reed and the Aggies were last year at this point in the season.

On the other hand, if the Tide struggles, or worse, loses, this weekend, there will be riots in the streets in Tuscaloosa.

While the Aggie offense has looked all season like Alabama did last weekend, their defense has been getting better each week, so don’t count them out (it’s not like Tennessee entered last week with an offense that was particularly functional, either).

What To Watch For:

  • Defensive improvement. Don’t look now, but Texas A&M’s pass defense is ranked No. 10 nationally. There’s some context to that, to be sure (giving up a lot on the ground and also some really subpar opponents), but the defense has looked like it’s been rounding into form after some pretty obvious early-season struggles. They’ll need to continue that upward trajectory and then some if they hope to pull out a victory this Saturday.
  • Any offense at all. Against LSU and Missouri, the A&M offense looked simply abysmal, failing to even score a touchdown. It may seem silly to expect significant improvement at this point (it is), but it’s what it will take for A&M to have a shot in this game.
  • Health? Texas A&M rested a number of players last week, with starters like WR Mario Craver, OG Trovon Baugh, DE Anto Saka and DT DJ Hicks not even suiting up. Will that rest prove fruitful against a Crimson Tide team coming off of games against Georgia and Tennessee? It’s a stretch, but hey, it could happen (flaps arms in a forced Angels in the Outfield reference).

Finally, here’s the weekly SEC shorts, if you can stomach getting to see Tennessee and Auburn gloat.

item.title: Fantasy Football Kicker Streamers: The 3 best pickups for Week 7
item.description: Denny Carter looks into which kickers have the best matchups headed into Week 7.
item.content:encoded:
Kickers are creatures of game script.

In fantasy football that doesn’t make them any different than a lot of running backs and wideouts and tight ends. For those positions, as with kicker, opportunity evaporates with unfriendly game script.

The receiver or tight end sees a dip in routes and targets when their team gets out to a big lead and runs the rock in the second half. The running back ends up with ten carries instead of twenty because his team has to abandon the run as they chase points in a trailing script. In an opportunity-based game, this is something short of ideal.

That’s why we want kickers in our lineups whose teams have a good chance of seeing plenty of neutral or positive game script. Usually this means a team won’t forgo easy field goal opportunities in the second half, down by multiple scores. So there is a process to selecting kickers — even those off the waiver wire.

In this space I’ll highlight a few waiver kicker options who check the boxes of a viable play. Some, of course, will be better than others. Oh, and one more thing: Accuracy doesn’t really matter at all. We want opportunity.

Week 6 Results

Here’s how our waiver wire kickers did in Week 6.

  • Chris Boswell: 17 points
  • Andy Boregales: 9 points
  • Cairo Santos: 8 points

Week 7 Kicker Options

Below is a look at kicker fantasy production allowed by each team through Week 6, along with a graph showing which coaches are most aggressive and most conservative with their fourth down decision making.

Ryan Fitzgerald (CAR) vs. Bucs

Tampa opponents this season have had multiple attempts in four of six games, thanks mostly to the Bucs being a stubbornly good red zone defense so far. It's the sort of bend-don't-break defense we seek in kicker matchups.

Fitzgerald has been a big-time beneficiary of the Panthers creating near-constant neutral and positive game script this season. Only nine teams have faced less negative game script than Carolina through Week 7. That should set up nicely for Fitzgerald here. We're going to keep streaming kickers against the Bucs until morale improves.

Jason Sanders (NYJ) vs. Dolphins

The Jets, as of this writing, are 2.5-point home favorites against the down impossibly bad Dolphins, who have given up multiple field goal tries in three of their past four games. No one has faced more negative game script than Miami through Week 6. I don't expect that to change this week with a Jets offense boosted by the return of Omar Cooper, Jr. and perhaps, one day, Adonai Mitchell.

@nyjets K Jason Sanders nails a 54-yard field goal in the pouring rain@CLEvsNYJ on CBS/Paramount+
Stream on @NFLPluspic.twitter.com/j5I53mjSSj

— NFL (@NFL) October 11, 2026

Sanders, fresh off a four field goal performance against the Patriots, is a legit high-upside swing this week.

Andy Borregales (NE) vs. Bears

We're going back to the Borregales well in what should be a high-scoring Thursday night affair, or as high scoring as a TNF game can be, I guess. Borregales has multiple attempts in three of six games and should benefit as the Patriots' red-hot red zone offense cools off a bit. That's what we saw in Week 6 against the Jets.

The Bears aren't a great matchup on paper — as seen above — but they have allowed three field goal tries in each of their two losses this season. Borregales should at least have a strong floor here.

item.title: Bills defense not better, but certainly different, in 2026
item.description: Pinpointing how this Bills defense is different through six games
item.content:encoded:
The Bills were always going to look different on defense in 2026.

From the time the firing of former head coach Sean McDermott was announced in the early parts of 2026, we all knew that Buffalo Bills owner Terry Pegula was pointing to coaching for a reason, and it wasn’t the performance of the team’s offense. So when new head coach and former offensive coordinator Joe Brady hired Jim Leonhard to be his defensive coordinator, everyone knew that qualitatively, what the Bills looked like on defense in 2026 would be very different than what the fans had been used to seeing from that unit for the previous nine years.

Through six weeks of the 2026 regular season, the Bills defense has absolutely looked different than it has in previous years. It’s also objectively been worse (data from Fantasy Points Data Suite).

The Buffalo defense thus far in 2026 is:

30th in EPA per play allowed
28th in EPA per drop back
25th in EPA per rush
28th in success rate against
28th in explosive play rate against

To put this in perspective, in 2025 in the same categories, the Bills were:

14th in EPA per play allowed
8th in EPA per drop back
31st in EPA per rush
11th in success rate against
25th in explosive play rate against

When your eyes tell you that the team has been a little better against the run than in 2025, your eyes are right. Everything else in terms of resultant defensive metrics is not just worse, but bad.

How did we get here? What’s different stylistically in 2026 versus previous years? The biggest and most glaring departure for the 2026 is that the Bills, for a decade one of the most nickel-stubborn teams in the National Football League, are now running base personnel 36.2% of their defensive snaps (9th in the NFL), up from single digit base defense percentages in most years of the Sean McDermott era. The increased base defensive percentage also leads to the Bills having an average box count of 7.13 (5th in the NFL), compared to 6.87 in 2025 (19th in the league) and 6.52 in 2024 (27th in the league). This heavier phenomenon is a contributing factor to the slightly increased effectiveness against the run, but it’s also a factor in the decreased effectiveness against the pass. the McDermott Bills were well-noted to be a team that refused to be dictated to in terms of defensive personnel, and former nickel defender Taron Johnson was the centerpiece of that philosophy that has changed under Jim Leonhard.

The next defensive characteristic that has changed significantly in 2026 on defense is the Bills coverage splits on defense. We live in a cover 3 league meta right now (current league average for cover 3 usage is 32.7%, the largest plurality of all coverage groups), but the Bills play cover 4 an astounding 26% of the time in 2026 (#1 in the league) while also being above league average in cover 3 usage (34.4% for Buffalo), which means over 60% of the time, the Bills are running either cover 3 or cover 4. Compare this to 2025, when the Bills ran cover 3 at a mark below the league average with cover 4 right at the league average and cover 2 and cover 1 above the league average. This shows that coverage diversity was far more present in 2025 versus 2026.

So the Bills are running a lot more base defense with heavier boxes and a lot more cover 3 and cover 4 (the most cover 4 in the league, even). You may think this is a more aggressive lean, but the Bills are pressing at least one receiver less in 2026 (14.1%, 28th in the league) than the “maligned for ‘soft coverage’” Sean McDermott’s defense in 2025 (30.2%, 7th in the NFL). “Maybe they’re blitzing more”, you say. I mean, a little bit. Buffalo is 20th in the NFL in blitz rate in 2026 (27.9%) and was 23rd in 2025 (24.3%), so not a statistically significantly difference.

If you have a team that is:

  1. running heavier defensive personnel
  2. running heavier boxes
  3. running the most cover 4 in the league
  4. running a less diverse selection of coverages
  5. pressing a lot less
  6. still not blitzing much

You have the 2026 Bills defense compared to the previous and most recent versions of it. And the results make sense: they’ve seen a slight uptick in run defense due to heavier boxes and heavier personnel, but they’re running a lot of cover 4 to prevent explosives, which might get them there if the communication in the back seven wasn’t leading to blown coverages, allowing explosive plays in the pass game despite the cover 4 calls. They’re not blitzing, they’re not pressing, they’re not diversifying, and they’re not disguising (26.3% disguise rate, 28th in the NFL), so quarterbacks aren’t holding the ball (2.68 average time to throw against, 11th in the NFL). Being able to stop the run from two high is the holy grail of NFL defenses (the Bills are top 12 in both two-high and base personnel usage), so you can see the outcome the Bills are trying to generate, but it’s not happening for them through six weeks.

The Bills were trying to get over the hump when they fired Sean McDermott, and they elected to hire a rookie head coach and a rookie defensive coordinator. You can’t do that and then logically not provide any grace for rookie mistakes from your rookie coaches, but the Bills are fortunate to be 5-1 going into their bye week with the defensive generating results this poor. Let’s hope we come out of the bye with a clear identity of how Jim Leonhard and the defense will get where we all want them to go.

…and that’s the way the cookie crumbles. I’m Bruce Nolan with Buffalo Rumblings. You can find me on Twitter and Instagram @BruceExclusive and look for new episodes of “The Bruce Exclusive” every Thursday on the Rumblings Cast Network — see more in my LinkTree!

item.title: How much is DeForest Buckner worth on the trade market?
item.description: DeForest Buckner is still one of the Colts’ best defensive players, but age and his contract complicate his trade value.
item.content:encoded:
This is the second part of a three-article series looking at the hypothetical trade value of three of the Colts’ biggest stars. This one is about DeForest Buckner. You can click here to read the previous one on Jonathan Taylor.

As with Taylor, this is not an argument that Indianapolis should trade Buckner. The Colts probably should not be looking to move any of these players unless the season falls apart or another team comes calling with an offer that is too good to ignore. The point of the series is simply to determine what these players would realistically be worth if serious trade interest developed around the deadline.

Buckner is an interesting case because the player is still very good, but almost everything surrounding him works against his value.

He is 32 years old. His contract voids after this season. Any team acquiring him would be doing so primarily for the stretch run and playoffs, with no guarantee he would remain there beyond February.

That makes this much more complicated than simply asking how good DeForest Buckner is.

Buckner is still really good

The easiest part of this evaluation is determining whether Buckner can still play. He definitely can.

Through six games, Buckner has four sacks, eight quarterback hits and 18 pressures. He consistently ranks amongst the highest interior defensive linemen in these categories. That is especially important considering the state of the Colts’ defensive front. Indianapolis has struggled badly to consistently pressure quarterbacks this season, yet Buckner continues to create problems from the interior. At 32 years old, he is still arguably the most dependable pass rusher on the roster. There has been no dramatic falloff where we are evaluating Buckner based on what he used to be. He is still collapsing pockets, still winning inside against the top interior offensive linemen and still capable of ruining a drive.

That puts him in a different category from the typical veteran defensive lineman available at the deadline.

The two trades that make sense as comparisons

There have been plenty of defensive tackles traded over the last decade, but very few are particularly useful here.

The best comparison is Leonard Williams. Seattle acquired Williams from the Giants at the 2023 trade deadline for a second-round pick in 2024 and a fifth-round pick in 2025. Williams was 29 and in the final year of his contract. Through eight games with the Giants that season, he had only 1.5 sacks. The Seahawks were 5-2, believed they could make a run and paid a significant price for a high-end interior defender.

The other useful comparison goes back to 2017, when Seattle acquired Sheldon Richardson from the Jets. The Seahawks sent a second-round pick and Jermaine Kearse while the teams also swapped seventh-round selections. Richardson was 26 at the time and coming off a season with 1.5 sacks, although he had already made a Pro Bowl and had an eight-sack season earlier in his career.

Both trades tell us that teams will pay substantial draft capital for an impact interior defensive lineman when they believe they are close to winning. From a performance standpoint, Buckner belongs in that conversation. He has already doubled Williams’ pre-trade sack total in three fewer games this season, and Richardson was coming off one of the quieter statistical seasons of his career when Seattle acquired him.

The problem is that Williams was 29 and Richardson was 26. Buckner is 32. That is an enormous difference when assigning trade value, even if Buckner is playing just as well or better than either player was at the time.

The contract makes him a potential rental

This is probably the biggest factor dragging Buckner’s value down.

His contract voids in February, which means a team trading for him would only control him for the remainder of the 2026 season unless it negotiated another deal. That could be eight or nine regular-season games plus the playoffs. The financial cost for this season would not be particularly difficult to handle.

Buckner has a $13 million base salary in 2026. The Colts already paid his $10 million roster bonus, and the prorated signing-bonus money would remain Indianapolis’ responsibility. A team acquiring him around the halfway point of the season would therefore be taking on roughly half of that $13 million salary, somewhere around $6.5 million depending on the exact date of the trade. Most contenders can find a way to absorb that, but the larger issue is what happens afterward.

There is no cheap year of team control waiting in 2027. There is no franchise-friendly contract that makes him a multi-year asset. The team either lets him reach free agency or has to negotiate a new contract with a player who will turn 33 next season.

That has to significantly reduce the return compared with Williams and Richardson.

How much does Buckner have left?

Age is a legitimate concern, but I would not assume Buckner is approaching the end. Defensive tackle is one of the positions where elite players can remain productive well into their 30s.

Cameron Heyward might be the most obvious example. He is 37 years old and was still one of the best defensive linemen in football last season. At age 36, PFF gave him the highest grade of any interior defender in the league at 90.4, and he earned another All-Pro selection. Heyward is obviously an extreme example, not the standard everyone should be expected to follow. Calais Campbell is still playing the position at 40!

Defensive tackle is a position that relies a lot on strength, technique and instincts and those 3 things don’t age. All of this shows that 32 is hardly ancient for a great defensive tackle. Buckner’s game also lends itself to aging relatively well. He is 6-foot-7, incredibly long and wins with power, technique and an ability to use his frame inside. He does not need to rely entirely on explosive athleticism to remain effective. I would be comfortable saying Buckner has at least a few quality seasons left if he remains healthy and if he decides he wants to play that long. There have been rumours about him retiring the last couple of seasons, so that also plays a factor into things.

A contender acquiring him would be doing so for the current playoff run first, but there is a legitimate possibility that the relationship could continue beyond that. If Buckner finishes the year playing at his current level, it would not be surprising at all to see him sign another multi-year contract.

The uncertainty simply means a team cannot value those future seasons as part of the trade itself.

Who could use Buckner?

Unlike Taylor, where only certain contenders have an obvious need at running back, the market for Buckner could be fairly broad.

Almost every playoff team could use another interior defender who can rush the quarterback, but 4 stand out to me.

Detroit would probably be the most interesting fit.

The Lions are 3-2 and clearly still view themselves as a championship contender. Aidan Hutchinson gives them a premier edge rusher, while Alim McNeill is a good interior player, but Detroit lost veteran nose tackle D.J. Reader during the offseason. Adding Buckner would give the Lions another proven interior pass rusher and allow them to build a defensive front capable of creating pressure without constantly blitzing. For a team with legitimate Super Bowl aspirations, Buckner is exactly the type of veteran addition that makes sense in October.

San Francisco would be the funniest destination for obvious reasons.

The 49ers traded Buckner to Indianapolis in 2020 because they did not want to give him the enormous contract he eventually received. Six years later, they could theoretically bring him back for a playoff push. San Francisco are amongst the NFL top teams and general manager John Lynch has already acknowledged that the 49ers are actively exploring the trade market. Their defensive line has also dealt with injuries, and the current interior group includes Osa Odighizuwa, Gracen Halton, Naquan Jones and Sebastian Valdez. Buckner already knows the organization, and Lynch has never been afraid to make an aggressive midseason move.

Chicago is another possibility.

The Bears are 4-2 and right in the middle of the NFC playoff picture. They currently rank in the top 10 in total defense, but the front could still use another legitimate interior pass-rushing threat, particularly with Montez Sweat currently unavailable. If Chicago believes it can legitimately contend this season, Buckner would give that defense another player capable of wrecking protections from the middle.

Then there is Denver.

The Broncos already have an excellent defensive front, so this is less about filling a glaring weakness. Zach Allen is one of the league’s better interior defenders and D.J. Jones gives them another veteran presence. Adding Buckner would simply make a strength borderline ridiculous. Denver is 4-2 and winning largely because of its defense. For a team built around stopping opponents and asking its offense to do enough, loading up on another high-end defensive lineman is not the craziest approach.

Those four would not be the only teams calling. That is what helps Buckner’s value. His position is valuable enough and his remaining salary is manageable enough that there should be multiple contenders capable of talking themselves into the move.

So, what is DeForest Buckner worth?

This is where the age and contract overpower the player evaluation.

If Buckner were 28 or 29, I think the Leonard Williams deal would be an excellent benchmark. A second-round pick with another late selection attached would make plenty of sense based on how Buckner is currently playing.

But he’s not 29. He is 32, the acquiring team gets no contractual control beyond this season, and it would have to decide almost immediately whether it wants to give another multi-year deal to a player entering his mid-30s. That is enough for me to knock the price down significantly.

My valuation would be:

A 2027 fourth-round pick.

That may sound low when you look strictly at the player. Buckner is considerably better than the average player traded for a fourth-round selection. If Indianapolis were simply ranking its best defensive players, he would be near the top.

Trade value is different. A team is paying for what it controls, not what Buckner has accomplished over the previous decade. In this case, it controls half a season and a playoff run, while assuming approximately $6.5 million in remaining salary and no guaranteed rights to the player afterward. Leonard Williams and Sheldon Richardson both fetched second-round picks plus additional value, but they were in their 20s and offered far more long-term upside. Buckner can still help a contender win a Super Bowl.

At 32 and months away from free agency, a fourth-round pick feels like the point where his current ability and his situation finally meet.

item.title: Panthers vs Eagles game review: Milestones
item.description: A well-earned victory came with a number of notable team and individual milestones.
item.content:encoded:
They can’t all be pretty. In fact, almost every game the Carolina Panthers have participated in this season has had a certain quality that only their fans can love. While the product on the field may have been ugly, there’s a certain aesthetic that having more wins than losses has that I think we can all appreciate.

While taking down the Philadelphia Eagles in their own building was the main goal, the Panthers set some personal records while a handful of players also made some history. For this weeks game review, let’s take a look at some of the records, milestones, and other notable marks that were reached.

Prior to kickoff, the Panthers social team put out a few things to watch with most coming to fruition.

Bryce Young became the first quarterback in team history to have at least 250 passing yards and a touchdown pass in seven consecutive games and the first player in the NFL since 2013 to throw for at least 280 yards and a touchdown in the first five games of the season. The last two of three quarterbacks to accomplish the same feat won MVP – Aaron Rodgers in 2011 and Peyton Manning in 2013.

On that note, the Young-led offense has score 146 points so far this season. This is the highest total through 5 games in team history, surpassing the old record of 135 set by Cam Newton and the 2015 Panthers on route to an MVP season and SB 50.

Tetairoa McMillan’s six receptions has him tied with Kelvin Benjamin as the second fastest player in team history to reach 100 career receptions. While not my favorite career-trajectory comparison, it is impressive nonetheless.

Speaking of great stats with frightening names tied to them, Ryan Fitzgerald’s first field goal of the afternoon made him the first kicker since big-legged Joey Slye to make the first 10 attempts in a season. Also, yes, Slye did also miss two extra points in that time.

Of course, there was also JJ Jansen setting the record for most games played by a long snapper in NFL history. Only another 100 more games to go until breaking the record for most games played in NFL history.

Of course, it can’t all be positive. The Panthers also set the team record for most penalty yardage given up in a single game. A worrying trend as the team has been near the top in penalties for the entire season and after a bye week they decided that wasn’t enough.

One last one to close out the fun. For the schadenfreude enjoyers: by beating the Eagles, the Panthers contributed to the NFC East being the first division in NFL history to have all their teams go winless in back-to-back weeks.

It’s hard to ignore the positive vibes permeating the team and their performance. A history of disappointment is sure to keep a sliver of nagging doubt in the back of the mind, but when the team is making history – the good kind, not the tragic kind – it’s bound to get people excited. Let’s see how things play out when the Panthers take on the division rival Tampa Bay Buccaneers next week. Until then, keep pounding.

item.title: Brock Purdy is the NFL's all-time record holder for highest career passer rating
item.description: The NFL has a new all-time record holder for highest career passer rating: Brock Purdy.
item.content:encoded:
The NFL has a new all-time record holder for highest career passer rating: Brock Purdy.

As of Monday night, Purdy has the highest passer rating in NFL history, at 105.6. To qualify for the official career record, a player needs to have thrown at least 1,500 passes in his NFL career, and on Monday night Purdy topped the 1,500-attempt mark, giving him the passer rating record.

In all, Purdy has completed 1,038 of 1,524 passes for 13,145 yards, with 98 touchdowns and 39 interceptions.

The record previously belonged to Ravens quarterback Lamar Jackson, who has a career passer rating of 102.7. He's followed by Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers at 101.8, Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow at 101.3 and Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes at 100.8. Purdy will probably keep the record for a while, as he's far enough ahead of the pack that no one would surpass him unless he has a disastrous end to the season while one of those quarterbacks behind him puts up record-setting numbers. There are also no other quarterbacks who are close to 1,500 pass attempts whose passer rating could surpass Purdy.

Passer rating is determined by a complex formula that combines completion percentage, yards per pass, touchdown percentage and interception percentage. The NFL adopted it as the league's official statistic for ranking passers in 1973. It's far from a perfect method of ranking quarterbacks — it ignores first downs, sacks, fumbles, rushing and other measurements of a player's quality — but as a rough gauge of how well a quarterback is playing, it's not bad. And it ranks Purdy ahead of every quarterback, ever.

item.title: 3 Reasons Why the Chicago Bears Won vs. the Falcons
item.description: With the return of some superheroes, Chicago traveled to Atlanta and got the W. Here are @BryanOrenchuk’s top 3 reasons why.
item.content:encoded:
The Chicago Bears traveled to Atlanta this week to take on the Falcons and imposed their will from start to finish. Here are my top three reasons Chicago won the game. Let’s get to it!

1. Competitive Fire

Call it competitive fire, juice, edge, ‘want-to,’ whatever works for you. From the opening kickoff through the closing seconds, the Chicago Bears simply wanted this game more than Atlanta. Despite what many people realize, that matters even at this level. Chicago came out to play in this one, and you could tell it meant something to them in all three phases. I’d be remiss not to mention the masses of Bears fans that traveled to Atlanta for this one too.

From the kickoff teams blowing up ball carriers, to the punt team perfectly executing some “Banana Balls” to Caleb Williams igniting the offense on the field or defense on the sidelines, these Bears were going to go down swinging. An encouraging sign after last week’s defeat at Lambeau. Zavier Scott looks like an absolute keeper on this team, and his juice on special teams stands out. Daniel Hardy had himself a game both in the third phase AND on Defense with Montez Sweat out. Noah Sewell made his presence felt as well and the contrast between what Kalif Raymond brings to what his predecessor Olamide Zacchaeus brought is night and day – and that’s only the reserve players! When you have your stars putting forth that same selfless effort to win games (spoiler alert – like the two guys listed below) then you have a fighters chance every week. And when your stars are as talented as they are in Chicago, good things can happen. REALLY good things. I might even call them super.

2. Iceman

Caleb heard all the noise, yes. But in my opinion, his biggest motivating factor is and has always been winning ball games as starting quarterback and leading his team to new heights. Well, he made quite the impression Sunday, completing over 80% of his passes with zero turnovers and 1 TD pass, in addition to a career-best mark for consecutive completions with 12 straight complete throws. And that doesn’t count the multiple throw aways he had either. Caleb was on fire. When he is healthy and playing like that, this offense will be hard to stop. Remember, Chicago didn’t even have their RB1B in Kyle Monangai this week either. I said it on Bears Over Beers last week that I hoped he learned from Case Keenum how explosive this offense can be even without him playing Superman in the pocket and not only did he allude to it leading up to this game, but it showed on the field. Chicago has playmakers at each position. All he has to do is get it to them. On Sunday, he did just that with EIGHT players securing at least 2 catches. Caleb is back, people. Cannot wait to see him at home this week against last year’s MVP runner-up and fellow 2024 rookie classman, Drake Maye. Expect fireworks.

3. Spidey

Not to be outdone by the epic return of Caleb Williams AKA Iceman, Kyler Gordon AKA “Spider Man” or “Spidey” had arguably the most impressive performance of the afternoon. Easing back into full-time action this week, Spidey played only 16 defensive snaps. In those snaps, he accumulated 4 tackles, 3 sacks, 3 tackles for a loss, 2 forced fumbles, and 2 QB hits. Spider Man is an absolute terror for opposing offenses, and we didn’t really even get to see him in coverage, where he is equally as dangerous.

After all he’s been through with the public outcry over missing so much action and reports of tension in the locker room, it was huge to see his performance this week and earn himself a game ball from Ben Johnson postgame. With the struggles this defense has had to start the season, particularly in the secondary, Gordon’s return couldn’t have come at a better time as Chicago has the Patriots, Seahawks, and Buccaneers before the Week 10 BYE – and ALL in Primetime.

What about you? What stood out most in your mind when watching The Beloved come away with the win?

item.title: Terry McLaurin believed to have season-ending knee injury
item.description: Commanders wide receiver Terry McLaurin had to be carted off the field with an air cast on his left knee on Monday night and the image didn't do much to conjure up hopes of a quick return to the field this season.
item.content:encoded:
Commanders wide receiver Terry McLaurin had to be carted off the field with an air cast on his left knee on Monday night and the image didn't do much to conjure up hopes of a quick return to the field this season.

Head coach Dan Quinn confirmed that the team feared a "significant" injury after the game and that McLaurin would go for tests on Tuesday to determine just how significant it is. Those tests are pending, but Ian Rapoport of NFL Media reports that the team is bracing to learn that McLaurin will miss the rest of the season.

McLaurin missed Week 4 with a hamstring injury and has 15 catches for 230 yards and a touchdown on the season.

McLaurin has two more years left on his contract and is set to have a $34 million cap number in 2027, but there's no guaranteed money left on the deal should the Commanders opt to move in a different direction.

item.title: Bengals progress report: Grading special teams
item.description: What grade do you think the Bengals’ special teams deserves at the bye?
item.content:encoded:
The Cincinnati Bengals are 3-2 coming out of their bye week, and depending on which side of the bed you wake up on, there’s plenty of reason for optimism or pessimism.

The offense has had its moments. The defense has had its moments. Unfortunately, so have the special teams, and not necessarily in a good way.

Outside of Evan McPherson, who apparently decided missing field goals is for lesser mortals, Darrin Simmons’ special teams units have been a frustrating combination of mediocrity and outright disaster.

Let’s start with the one guy who’s been keeping the lights on.

Field Goal/Field Goal Block

With 11 guys on the field working together, every play has a lot of moving pieces, but the field-goal unit is fairly simple. As long as the long snapper, holder, and kicker do their jobs, everyone else just needs to keep the defense out of the way for a second or two.

Outside of a penalty that pushed the Bengals out of field-goal range, Evan McPherson and the rest of the field-goal unit have been perfect.

McPherson now owns the franchise record for most consecutive field goals made with 22, a streak that stretches back to the 2025 season. In 2026, McPherson is a perfect 10-for-10. What’s most impressive, though, is that five of those kicks have come from 50 or more yards, with a long of 58.

Obviously, the offense wants to walk away from every drive with seven points, but that’s not always possible. The Bengals are extremely fortunate to have a kicker who is so accurate from beyond 50 yards. Nobody really cares about the kicker until a field goal can win or lose the game in the final minutes.

On the defensive side of things, the only major issue so far this season came in Week 5. Dexter Lawrence was flagged for roughing the snapper against the Dolphins, giving Miami a fresh set of downs after a successful field goal. The Dolphins eventually scored a touchdown, turning three points into seven.

The Bengals won that game, but those four additional points helped keep Miami within striking distance late in the fourth quarter.

Field Goal Unit: 98% (A+)
Field Goal Block Unit: 85% (B)
Overall Field Goal Unit: 92% (A-)

Punt/Punt Return

Here’s where the real problems begin.

As far as punt coverage goes, the first major mistake came in Week 3 against the Steelers. The Bengals’ defense stopped Pittsburgh in the third quarter and forced a punt, but Cedric Johnson was called for an obvious roughing-the-kicker penalty. That gave the Steelers a fresh set of downs, and what should have been a defensive stop turned into a Pittsburgh touchdown a few plays later.

In the same game, former punt returner Ke’Shawn Williams muffed a punt that Pittsburgh recovered at the Bengals’ 14-yard line. The defense managed to hold the Steelers to a field goal, but instead of Cincinnati getting the ball back with an opportunity to score, Pittsburgh walked away with three points.

Those two mistakes handed the Steelers possessions that resulted in 10 points in a game the Bengals lost by three.

Ryan Rehkow’s punting, meanwhile, has been unspectacular. His 44.9 yards-per-punt average ranks among the lowest in the NFL. Nine of his 16 punts have been downed inside the 20-yard line, and he hasn’t recorded a touchback.

There haven’t been any major mistakes on Rehkow’s part, but his overall production has been below average.

The real issue with this unit isn’t necessarily the punter. It’s the mistakes being made around him. A roughing penalty and a muffed punt aren’t just bad plays. They’re the kinds of mistakes that can cost a team a game, and against Pittsburgh, they helped do exactly that.

Punting Unit: 74% (C)
Punt Return Unit: 49% (F)
Overall Punting grade: 61 (D-)

Kickoff/Kickoff Return

Kickoffs are so different now than they used to be. With touchbacks generally bringing the ball out to the 35-yard line, teams have more incentive to kick short of the end zone and force a return. That means more opportunities for explosive plays, but it also means more opportunities for mistakes.

For the Bengals, the most glaring mistake came in Week 5 against the Dolphins.

Rookie wide receiver Dohnte Meyers fielded a kickoff at the four-yard line, but his momentum carried him out of bounds almost immediately, setting Joe Burrow and the offense up in the shadow of their own goalposts.

The offense managed to move the ball out near midfield, but the drive ultimately ended with a punt. While the mistake didn’t directly cost Cincinnati points, it put the offense in a difficult position and eliminated any chance of starting that possession with favorable field position.

To be fair, Meyers also started that game with an 81-yard kickoff return that set the Bengals up at Miami’s 10-yard line. Burrow and the offense took advantage, scoring a touchdown just three plays later.

That’s the frustrating thing about the kickoff return unit. There’s clearly potential for big plays, but the execution hasn’t always been consistent.

On the coverage side, the Bengals haven’t suffered any major breakdowns comparable to what we’ve seen from the punt units. They’ve generally done a respectable job of limiting opposing returners and avoiding the kind of disastrous plays that can completely flip field position.

Kickoff Unit Grade: 82% (B-)
Kickoff Return Unit Grade: 79% (C+)
Overall Kickoff/Return Grade: 80%(B-)

Darrin Simmons has been the Bengals’ special teams coordinator since 2003. He was named assistant head coach in 2020 and has held both positions ever since. Special teams typically haven’t been a major problem for the Bengals under Simmons, but this season has been different. Outside of McPherson, the unit has made several costly mistakes, and some have had a direct impact on the outcome of games.

Look no further than Pittsburgh.

The Bengals lost that game by three points, and two special teams mistakes gave the Steelers possessions that resulted in 10 points. It’s impossible to say with certainty how the game would have unfolded without those errors, but it’s hard not to wonder what Cincinnati’s record would look like if those mistakes hadn’t happened.

It’s not all on Simmons. Players have to execute, and there are only so many things a coach can control once the ball is snapped. However, Simmons is responsible for preparing his units, and right now, those units aren’t consistently getting the job done.

A 4-1 record, including a 1-0 start in the division, would sound a hell of a lot better than 3-2.

Hopefully, the Bengals got things straightened out during the bye week. Because without McPherson’s excellence, Cincinnati’s special teams would be earning a solid D.

Overall Defensive Grade: 77% C

item.title: Examining the roster ties between Patriots, Bears ahead of Week 7
item.description: The ex-Patriots and ex-Bears in the fold for Week 7 at Soldier Field.
item.content:encoded:
The connections extend beyond coaches Thomas Brown, Ashton Grant, Jason Houghtaling, Charles London and Isaiah Ford.

Between the active rosters, practice squads and reserve lists, three former New England Patriots and four former Chicago Bears find themselves in the fold Thursday’s primetime meeting at Soldier Field.

Here’s a glance through those on-field ties heading into the 8:15 p.m. ET kickoff.

CHICAGO

Joe Thuney, guard — A future inductee into the Pro Football Hall of Fame, Thuney’s NFL run began in Foxborough in the third round of the 2016 draft at No. 78 overall. The North Carolina State All-American earned Super Bowl LI and LIII rings during his versatile stay on the offensive line and made the cut for the Patriots’ All-2010s and All-Dynasty teams. A five-year deal brought Thuney to the Kansas City Chiefs as an unrestricted free agent in 2021 after playing on the franchise tag. And last March, after adding Super Bowl LVII and LVIII rings to his collection, the 33-year-old ironman was traded into quarterback Caleb Williams’ pass protection and signed a two-year extension. Thuney has started 167 games in the regular season and 23 games in the postseason during his career. The four-time Pro Bowler and five-time All-Pro stands as the reigning NFL Protector of the Year and a captain.

Garrett Bradbury, center — Before NFL free agency opened in March, Bradbury’s stay at Gillette Stadium reached its end with one year remaining on his contract. The Patriots agreed to trade the 31-year-old center to the Bears in exchange for a fifth-round draft choice in 2027 on the heels of Pro Bowler Drew Dalman’s retirement. Bradbury had started every game for the reigning AFC champions from September into February, handling 98 percent of the offensive snaps. Signing in 2025 after being released by the Minnesota Vikings, he received the organization’s Ron Hobson Good Guy Award on the way to Super Bowl LX. The former Rimington Trophy winner out of North Carolina State has started all 111 of his appearances in the regular season since being selected in the first round at No. 18 overall in 2019.

Jamree Kromah, defensive end — A 26-year-old former transfer from Rutgers to James Madison, Kromah entered the NFL with Chicago as an undrafted rookie in 2024. The defensive end agreed to depart from the Bears’ practice squad for a spot on the Patriots’ 53-man roster in September of his rookie campaign. And after spending three weeks among the team’s inactives, which marks the league’s minimum requirement for poaching, he was waived and soon circled back to his previous club. Kromah made initial 53-man roster for the first time out of training camp and debuted last Sunday.

NEW ENGLAND

Lorenz Metz, offensive tackle — The Patriots signed the 29-year-old Metz to the practice squad ahead of the AFC divisional round in January. A futures contract followed. And after the 53-man roster deadline passed in August, so did a return to the practice squad as an exempt 17th member via the NFL International Pathway. Born in Bavaria, Germany, the offensive tackle played collegiately at Cincinnati and went undrafted in 2023. The Bears marked his first stop in the league. After being waived at the start of his rookie training camp, Metz went on to spend two campaigns on the practice squad of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Matt Pryor, guard — Signed off the practice squad of the Arizona Cardinals, Pryor landed on the 53-man roster in Foxborough as the calendar turned to October and checked in at guard last week. The veteran out of Texas Christian has appeared in 111 games, including 40 starts, since being selected by the Philadelphia Eagles in the sixth round of the 2018 NFL draft at No. 206 overall. He has also been an Indianapolis Colt and a San Francisco 49er. And in 2024, Pryor became a Bear on a one-year deal. The 31-year-old saw action in every game that campaign in the NFC North while making 15 starts.

Kindle Vildor, cornerback — After serving as a standard elevation amid attrition at cornerback, the Patriots signed Vildor to the 53-man roster in early October. The 28-year-old’s time in the AFC East has included six tackles, including one for loss, to go with one pass deflection and one forced fumble. Signed in March and retained on the practice squad in August, Vildor originally entered the league with the Bears in the fifth round of the 2020 draft at No. 163 overall. The Georgia Southern product spent time with five other organizations before heading to Foxborough. Through 83 appearances, including 27 starts, he has had a hand in 146 tackles, one sack, two forced fumble and two interceptions.

Kevin Byard III, safety — Voted a team captain following the preseason, the 33-year-old Byard reunited with a familiar staff in March after leading the NFL with seven interceptions with the Bears in 2025. A three-time Pro Bowler and first-team All-Pro, he has appeared in 170 games and made 161 starts since entering the league out of Middle Tennessee State in the third round of the 2016 draft. Setting out with head coach Mike Vrabel’s former Tennessee Titans before being dealt to Philadelphia ahead of the 2023 trade deadline, the veteran safety has amassed 998 tackles, 36 interceptions, six sacks, four forced fumbles, six fumble recoveries and two touchdowns off turnovers to the tune of 424 return yards.

item.title: Ravens discussion: should Eric DeCosta make a trade with the Colts?
item.description: The Colts are in disarray. Should the Ravens swoop in and trade for an impact veteran?
item.content:encoded:
The Indianapolis Colts fired general manager Chris Ballard on Monday after a 2-4 start to the 2026 season, stirring speculation that the team could engage in a fire sale before the trade deadline.

Baltimore Ravens general manager Eric DeCosta already made one blockbuster trade, sending a second-round pick to the Philadelphia Eagles in exchange for center Cam Jurgens. But the Colts have their own treasure trove of players to offer, particularly in the trenches where DeForest Buckner and Quenton Nelson can change games on their own. Should DeCosta call up Colts assistant GM Chris Dodds and make another deal?

Nikhil Mehta

If the Ravens want to move on from John Simpson as their starting left guard, they will have to stomach paying him $17.5 million for roughly half a season of work. Quenton Nelson would no doubt be a massive upgrade, but he is due for a substantial raise once his contract expires after the season. He would also cost premium draft capital – if Jurgens went for a second-round pick, Nelson is probably worth a first. It just does not make sense for Baltimore.

Buckner, though, I have coveted for years. Officially, he already has four sacks and four tackles for loss through six games, and according to Pro Football Focus, he ranks ninth among interior defenders with 19 pressures. His pass rushing opportunities have also been somewhat limited by the Colts trailing for most of their games to open the year. This is another expiring contract in an expensive market, though, so a premium Day 3 pick would be the most I would offer for a half-season rental.

Dustin Cox

As much as I love the idea of adding Quinton Nelson to the Ravens, I simply do not think it is feasible given the combination of draft capitol required to pry him away from the Colts and the need to pay him a new contract. Nelson will surely demand another top-of-the-market deal and I am not sure if the Ravens are in a spot to hand one out, given their future cap situation and players such as Roger Rosengarten and Nate Wiggins who will be eligible for extensions next year. A player such as DeForest Buckner may make more sense, but Baltimore already has big-contract players on the defensive line in Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones. Already giving up a 2028 second-round pick for Cam Jurgens means Eric DeCosta may not be as willing to part with another Day 2 pick. If a trade is to be made before the deadline, I expect DeCosta to flip a mid-round pick for a solid player instead.

Zach Canter

The Ravens should absolutely be calling to see the asking price on Quinton Nelson and DeForest Buckner. Both are north of 30 and on expiring contracts that the Colts should be looking to offload. I could see the Ravens passing on Buckner cause they have both Nnamdi Madubuike and Travis Jones signed long-term. Jesse Minter has struggled to get the most out of his pass rush, particularly with Trey Hendrickson and Mike Green failing to produce at the same time. Another disruptive interior would boost the pass rush and offer the flexibility for Madubuike to flex outside as a jumbo edge rusher.

Nelson is a guy the Ravens shouldn’t be outbid for. There are a ton of resources now tied up in the offensive line: a first round pick in Ioane, the trade for Jurgens (and his contract), and veteran deals for John Simpson and Ronnie Stanley. Roger Rosengarten is eligible for an extension next spring and should be in line for a substantial raise. But with Stanley on an expiring contract and Vinson looking plausible as a future left tackle, there’s no reason for the Ravens to not go all in on building the wall this year and the future. There’s a very possible future that includes Nelson, Jurgens, Ioane, and Rosengarten the core of the OL for the next couple of years. Restructure a couple contracts, throw John Simpson in the deal, extend Lamar Jackson this offseason, and there’s a way to make the cap space for both Nelson and Rosengarten to get extensions. If the Ravens want to be a contender this year, it’s a move they should absolutely make. As the L.A. Rams say, F them picks.

Kevin McNelis

The Colts are in significant disarray at the moment, and Chris Ballard’s firing seems to signify that they’re ready to head in a new direction. With that in mind, I agree that Baltimore should see what the asking price is for Quenton Nelson and/or DeForest Buckner. The earlier acquisition of Cam Jurgens for a future second-rounder seems to signify that Baltimore is willing to deal at a high price to try to win now; the question is what kind of price they’re willing to pay for either of these guys, considering that they’d be short-term rentals under their current contracts.

My gut says the Colts stand pat for at least a few more days while they try to figure out who is handling any trade considerations, especially given EDC’s track record of swooping in like a hawk to go after embattled franchises at moments of vulnerability. If I had to pick one target over the other, I’d see what the Colts want for Quenton Nelson since he would shore up the line basically everywhere barring another injury. Q is one of the most reliable guards in the league and has been for many years, so if you could line up LJ’s return with reinforcements along his line, this offense could get a huge, much-needed boost.

I don’t know that I see the Ravens actually pulling the trigger to go after of these guys, but I’ve been surprised before (the Roquan acquisition comes to mind).

item.title: Cowboys news: Stephen Jones gives full support to Brian Schottenheimer

The Dallas Cowboys came out against the Green Bay Packers on Sunday night needing a win in the worst way. Instead, the defense spent the first half looking like they didn’t learn anything from their previous loss, putting the team in a 17-0 hole. The offense never really fully woke up to respond, and anything they did do well was far too late, especially after two turnovers.

This team being 2-4 as a result has called into question every single aspect of the coaching that’s supposed to have them prepared for gamedays, but isn’t right now.

Stephen Jones says Brian Schottenheimer has full support of Cowboys’ ownership – Todd Archer, ESPN

Brian Schottenheimer is on the hot seat as far as fans are concerned, but the Joneses say it isn’t so.

Twenty-three games into his tenure as the Dallas Cowboys head coach, Brian Schottenheimer has a 9-13-1 record and the full support of ownership.

“Absolutely. There’s not any question in Jerry’s and I’s mind,” executive vice president Stephen Jones said Monday on 105.3 The Fan in Dallas. “He has the team. There’s no question they want to go out there and execute and make things happen. We feel really good … about our coaching staff. We just have to continue to evolve and get to a point where we can win these football games.”

Cowboys’ Christian Parker hire looks worse than ever after Jonathan Gannon revenge game – Jerry Trotta, The Landry Hat

Jonathan Gannon continues to dominate the Cowboys offense every time he gets a chance to coach against it.

Gannon had already built a long track record of coaching successful defenses, most notably in Philadelphia. The Eagles fielded one of the NFL’s best defenses during their run to the Super Bowl in 2022, and he had Arizona punching above its weight class for most of his tenure.

One variable the Cowboys clearly overlooked was Gannon’s history against Dak Prescott. There’s a misconception that Vic Fangio gives Prescott the most fits of any defensive play-caller, when Gannon is actually the Prescott Stopper. Sunday night hammered that home.

Pro Bowl WR blames ‘mid OC’ Schottenheimer for Cowboys’ struggles – Todd Brock, The Cowboys Wire

The evidence is building that HC Brian Schottenheimer is simply in over his head right now.

Much of the focus is starting to land on Schottenheimer as the offensive play-caller. Now 9-13-1 since taking the head coaching job in Dallas, many within Cowboys Nation are now openly calling for a change and wondering if Schottenheimer was ever the offensive mastermind he was marketed to be.

The normally reliable connections with CeeDee Lamb and George Pickens were off. Prescott completed only 15 of 29 throws to the duo, and both of the turnovers were on throws to Lamb, who slipped on his route leading to the second pick.

item.title: FOOTBALL COURT: Is Bryce Young is the NFL MVP so far?
item.description: James Dator and Mark Schofield debate who the NFL MVP is so far in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
This NFL season is completely off the rails in the best way possible. Nothing is predictable, all our assumptions have been torn asunder, and somehow we’re sitting at the end of Week 6 with there being very real, sensible discussions over whether Bryce Young is on pace to win the NFL MVP award.

Young has become the league’s most-talked about quarterback (at least in a positive way). He’s absolutely balling out in year four, playing almost mistake-free football, with his only two interceptions being on final plays of the half or drive where they were chalked up as true desperation plays. Meanwhile he’s moving the ball vertically better than almost anyone in the league, and is on pace to finish with 5,267 yards, 37 TDs, and 7 INTs — all while cementing the Panthers as the best team in the NFC South, with everyone else lagging far behind.

That’s just the resume, and here comes the rub: Does this all mean that Bryce Young is worthy of the MVP award if he keeps up this level of play? Now we send this for ruling in FOOTBALL COURT, where James Dator and Mark Schofield make our cases on both sides of this debate. Think of it like a text-based First Take, except there’s less yelling, and 200% more dads who are very concerned about whether our fall grass will become established before the first frost.

Bryce Young deserves the MVP — James Dator

I will concede that it’s very early to have this discussion, but I’m hard-pressed to find anyone else who contends for the award this year. We know this has become a purely QB-based award, which is ridiculous — but it’s the state of football.

What Bryce Young is doing for the Panthers is unprecedented. This season Young has had one of the worst offensive lines in football, allowing pressure on 44.5% of dropbacks, and giving him only 1.9 seconds of pocket time on average. These are the standard death knells of a good passing offense, but Young’s unreal processing speed in the pocket is still allowing him to throw players open and generate big plays.

Young has completed 21 passes of 20+ yards this season, which ranks him 7th in the NFL — despite all six guys above him playing one more game, due to the Panthers’ early bye. Averaging over four 20+ yard passes per game is preposterous when there’s not solid blocking in front of you, but it’s still happening every game.

When we talk about “Most Valuable” it should be defined by a player doing something that no other team in the NFL could if you replace that player with another. The Bears, for instance, still managed to win two of their three games without Caleb Williams under center, amassing over 375 yards of offense in those two wins. Case Keenum was able to run the offense well, Tyson Bagent less so — but there’s still an argument to be made that Ben Johnson makes life easy for his quarterbacks with scheme.

With Bryce Young and the Panthers nobody could do what Young is doing. If you stuck any other quarterback in the role that he’s in right now they would be toast, throwing multiple picks a game because they’re under so much duress while trying to move the ball downfield. Instead he’s not just setting franchise records in Carolina, he’s cementing himself among the most elite players of the last two decades.

Do you know what 2011 Aaron Rodgers and 2013 Peyton Manning had in common? They both won the NFL MVP. If we look at Carolina’s remaining schedule, there’s ample room for big games from Bryce Young with two games remaining against the Saints, two against Tampa Bay, the Falcons and the Steelers. It’s entirely possible we see his numbers go up even further, especially as more offensive linemen get healthy for the Panthers — and if that all happens, then he’s a lock to win this award.

Ok, but seriously? — Mark Schofield

At the outset, it speaks volumes that we are even entertaining this conversation. Not because of what it says about the rest of the NFL this season, but what it says about Young himself.

This is a quarterback that was benched at the start of the 2024 season and replaced by Andy Dalton. That we are here, two calendar years later, taking seriously his credentials as a potential MVP says a lot about both Young himself, and the job the coaching staff has done with him, and what the front office has done around him.

That being said …

Becoming part of the conversation is one thing, winning it is yet another. Young has certainly done some impressive things this year (the statistic linked above about quarterbacks throwing for 280 yards and at least one touchdown in each of their first five games certainly puts him in some rarified company) but look who Young has put those numbers up against:

The Chicago Bears
The Atlanta Falcons
The Cleveland Browns
The Detroit Lions
The Philadelphia Eagles

That those teams are a combined 15-14 is just part of the story. Those are also some poor pass defenses. Looking at Adjusted Net Yards per Attempt, the Eagles clock in with an ANY/A allowed of 6.6 (11th worst in the NFL), the Lions at 7.0 (9th worst in the NFL) and the Bears clock in with an ANY/A allowed of 7.3 (6th worst in the NFL).

The Lions are allowing a league-worst 297.4 yards per game through the air, with the Falcons not too far behind in fifth, allowing an average of 252.0 yards per game through the air.

Again, this is not to discredit what Young has done this year, but to give it some context. Also, consider this chart, which sets out Expected Points Added per Dropback and Completion Percentage Over Expectation, as created by RBSDM:

Is Young in a very good spot? One would say that being in a cluster with Patrick Mahomes, Trevor Lawrence, and C.J. Stroud is good company.

But some other quarterbacks on this chart are in a better position, namely Brock Purdy and 2025 MVP Josh Allen.

Keeping with Purdy for a moment, and addressing the very valid point of playing in the face of pressure. As charted by Pro Football Focus this season, Young has been pressured on 44.5% of his dropbacks, which is fourth-most in the NFL. This certainly gives some context to what Young has done, and it does work in his favor. On those plays Young has posted an Adjusted Completion Percentage of 62.5%, stripping out throwaways and drops, and completed 42.2% of his passes for 510 yards, four touchdowns, and a pair of interceptions.

Now let’s look at what Purdy has done when pressured. While he has not been pressured to the same extent as Young — on only 32.3% of his dropbacks — he completed 53.7 of his passes for 287 yards and a touchdown when pressured, without an interception.

He has also posted an ACP of 68.6% when pressured this year, and the 49ers are currently 6-0 following Monday night’s game against the Washington Commanders. So those pressure numbers may change once full charting is completed.

Is Young in the conversation?

Sure.

But is he the MVP?

Not so fast, my friends.

YOU BE THE JUDGE

Let us know in the comments which side you fall on. Is Bryce Young the NFL MVP through Week 6, is it Brock Purdy, Josh Allen, or is there another dark horse worthy of mention?

item.title: John Harbaugh to Giants RBs: ‘Do something … take the job’
item.description: Harbaugh challenges his running backs to win the RB1 job.
item.content:encoded:
New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh has a clear message for the team’s running backs, stuck in a four-way timeshare that is not producing results anyone is happy with.

“Do something.”

After getting four carries for just 2 yards on Sunday against the New Orleans Saints despite starting the game, Najee Harris expressed his frustration.

“It’s hard to get in a rhythm with one or two plays. The first couple runs will be like, ‘OK, how are they playing it?’ And then the next ones will be, ‘OK, this is how you attack it.’ But if you’re getting a play here and then get taken out for a series, there’s nothing you could do. That’s why I’m saying, ‘I don’t know.’ I’ve never been through none of this before.”

At the end of a Monday Zoom call with Harbaugh dominated by the impending decision regarding whether Jameis Winston or J.J. McCarthy will be the team’s starting quarterback, I asked Harbaugh if he understood Harris’s frustratio and what, if anything, he would do about the backfield timeshare.

“Do understand it. Respect it. Also understand that that’s earned,” Harbaugh said. “I would love for us to be in that kind of a circumstance. A (Baltimore Ravens running back) Derrick Henry circumstance or a (Philadelphia Eagles running back) Saquon Barkley circumstance or whatever it might be. That would be great, and we haven’t. Our run game hasn’t earned that yet, and none of those guys have.”

Harbaugh had acknowledged on Sunday night that trying to split carries between four backs is not ideal.

“Now you can argue that. You can say, well, I don’t like that. I don’t like you divvying up the snaps between four backs. And I can tell you, I don’t like it either,” Harbaugh said. “One of those guys needs to step up. Somebody needs to step up and be the back. And none of those guys have done that yet. And when one of those guys steps up to be the back, then they’ll be the back. That’s your answer.”

The Giants are 22nd in the NFL averaging 3.8 yards per carry. Nearly all of their big plays in the run game have come from quarterbacks or wide receivers on jet sweeps or reverses. Cam Skattebo’s 19-yard run is the longest by a Giants’ running back this season.

Here are the rushing numbers:

  • Skattebo: 81 carries, 294 yards, 3.6 yards per carry
  • Harris: 31 carries, 99 yards, 3.2 yards per carry
  • Tyrone Tracy: 13 carries, 40 yards, 3.1 yards per carry
  • Devin Singletary: 13 carries, 39 yards, 3.0 yards per carry

“My advice would be to any player, and it’s all the guys, we had the same conversation. I’ve had the same conversation with all the running backs, the receivers, it’s no different than any position, but do the most you can with the opportunities you get,” Harbaugh said. “Make the most of those opportunities and you’re sure to get more opportunities. Do something.

“So, I get it that you want to get out there and you want to get a rhythm, but that rhythm is earned, too, and it just hasn’t happened yet. Definitely want it to happen. A couple weeks ago, we kind of went that direction and the running game was no different than it was this last game.”

Skattebo is the only back with double-digit carries in a game, and he reached that number in every game before being mostly sidelined and never touching the ball in Sunday’s loss to the New Orleans Saints. He has had mixed success, only averaging at least 4 yards per carry in one game without Jaxson Dart at quarterback. His four fumbles in five gamed led Harbaugh to look elsewhere against the Saints.

Harbaugh did not take issue with Harris expressing his frustration.

“I respect that he said that,” Harbaugh said. “I mean, I get it. Shoot, that’s how we all want it. That’s for sure and I respect that he would want that, too.”

Who Harbaugh and the Giants turn to when they hand the ball off on Sunday against the Houston Texans is anybody’s guess.

“I do know that each of the guys, because I’ve talked to all those guys, is they want to be that guy. They’re not advocating for the other guy to be that guy. They’re advocating for themself to be that guy,” Harbaugh said. “My advice is go out there and take the job when you get the ball. Take the job.”

item.title: Eagles star Hurts could miss season over blood clots
item.description: Jalen Hurts may not play again in 2026 for the struggling Philadelphia Eagles after being diagnosed with multiple blood clots in his lungs.
item.content:encoded:
Week six in the NFL produced one of the biggest stories of the campaign so far, with the struggling Philadelphia Eagles possibly losing quarterback Jalen Hurts for the rest of the season.

Hurts has been diagnosed with multiple blood clots in his lungs and, in his absence, the Eagles were beaten by the Carolina Panthers.

There were also unlikely heroes as the Arizona Cardinals pulled off the biggest upset of the season so far.

Kicker Chad Ryland scored all of Arizona's points at the Los Angeles Rams to leave the former Super Bowl favourites bottom of the NFC West division.

Elsewhere, the Kansas City Chiefs remain unbeaten, the Cleveland Browns maintained their surprise start and the Houston Texans concluded this year's London series by winning a thriller at Wembley.

Here are five things you need to know from Sunday's action.

Eagles lose as Hurts ruled out

The Eagles were already struggling with injuries before last Sunday's loss to Jacksonville at Tottenham.

They then revealed that quarterback Hurts played that game with a superficial blood clot in his calf, and a follow-up ultrasound showed it had moved, so back-up Tanner McKee came in for his third NFL start at home to the Carolina Panthers.

Tight end Tommy Tremble scored his first two touchdowns of the season as the Panthers won 25-14, meaning the Eagles have lost four straight games for the first time since Nick Sirianni became head coach in 2021.

It was then revealed on Monday that Hurts has been diagnosed with "deep vein thrombosis, as well as bilateral pulmonary emboli", which means he has multiple blood clots in his lungs.

The 2025 Super Bowl MVP is having treatment and his recovery will take at least three months. NFL Network's Ian Rapoport has reported Hurts is expected to miss the rest of the season and that he was advised by doctors not to sleep as a precautionary measure.

As a result, Hurts had not slept for 36 hours when the game against the Jaguars in London started.

The Eagles also lost offensive linemen Lane Johnson (retirement) and Cam Jurgens (traded to Baltimore) two weeks ago.

After reaching two of the past four Super Bowls, many Philly fans fear this could be the end of an era.

Rams need to stop the rot

The Los Angeles Rams started the season as the clearest Super Bowl favourites in nine years but were replaced by the San Francisco 49ers after last Monday's overtime defeat by the Buffalo Bills.

They cut kicker Harrison Mevis on Tuesday and signed Blake Grupe from the New York Jets' practice squad, and although Grupe's field goal opened the scoring against Arizona, he injured a knee while making a tackle from the ensuing kick-off.

The Rams edged back in front with 47 seconds remaining as punter Ethan Evans took on the kicking duties to add the extra point after Colby Parkinson's touchdown.

But Arizona hit straight back and a career-high sixth field goal by Chad Ryland clinched an 18-16 win as time expired.

After just three wins last season, the Cardinals now have two this year and both have come at SoFi Stadium having also beaten the Los Angeles Chargers in week one.

Arizona also crept above the Rams in a division which features the unbeaten 49ers and defending champions the Seattle Seahawks.

"We've got to be able to figure it out and it starts with me," said the Rams' head coach Sean McVay.

Walker continues to set pace

Kansas City Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes reached 100 regular-season wins in his 131st start, tying Tom Brady's record.

After missing out on last season's play-offs, the Chiefs boosted their roster by signing the Super Bowl's Most Valuable Player Kenneth Walker and he rushed for another 128 yards and two touchdowns in Sunday's 22-6 win over the Chargers.

The running back now leads the NFL with 665 rushing yards, a record from a player's first five games with a new team, and the Chiefs visit his former team Seattle next Sunday.

Kansas City and the Minnesota Vikings are now 5-0 while San Francisco - the only other unbeaten team after five wins - are at home to Washington on Monday night.

The Buffalo Bills held on for a 33-30 win at the Las Vegas Raiders to improve to 5-1 while Caleb Williams returned from a hamstring injury to help the Chicago Bears to a 31-23 win at the Atlanta Falcons.

  • 'Ran through me' & 'good value in pub' - ex-NFL star Kelce tries rugby

Hunter pulls off rare feat at Wembley

After last week's last-gasp win over the Eagles, it was a role reversal for the Jacksonville Jaguars as they remained in London to face the Houston Texans.

The divisional match-up produced the highest-scoring London game since 2015, with Ka'imi Fairbairn's field goal securing a 34-31 win for Houston, but it was a landmark day for Jacksonville's Travis Hunter.

The second overall draft pick in 2025, Hunter came into the league determined to become its first full-time two-way player in 30 years and in his 13th NFL game, he made a significant impact on both offence and defence for the first time.

The 23-year-old, who plays as a wide receiver and cornerback, became the first player to claim a touchdown catch and an interception in the same game since Brian Dawkins (Philadelphia Eagles) in 2002 – and the fourth since the league merger in 1970.

Hunter made both plays in the fourth quarter, with his pick leading to a Cam Little field goal which made it 31-31, before Fairbairn clinched Houston's second win of the season while the Jags slipped to 4-2.

Browns are surprise division leaders

The Baltimore Ravens had a divisional clash at the Cleveland Browns and star running back Derrick Henry had a crucial fumble in the fourth quarter.

That allowed Cleveland running back Audric Estime, who started the week on Minnesota's practice squad, to punch in a touchdown before Andre Szmyt's second game-winning field goal in three weeks gave the Browns a 13-10 victory.

After being booed by Cleveland fans in pre-season, quarterback Deshaun Watson has now led the Browns to a 4-2 start and they are surprise leaders of the AFC North on a tie-breaker.

Baltimore and the Pittsburgh Steelers are also 4-2, with the Steelers having come back from 16-3 down in the fourth quarter to win 26-19 in overtime at the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Next up for Cleveland is a trip to the Tennessee Titans, who fought back in the final quarter to beat the Indianapolis Colts 26-20 for their first victory of the season.

That means the only teams without a win are the Miami Dolphins (0-5) and the Los Angeles Chargers (0-6).
